| [CLAIM-993](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-993.md) | In small ReLU networks the barrier that survives alignment is set by width, by the group quotiented and by the path family, and does not sort pairs by the input cue they rely on | What [CASE-385](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-385.md) measured, stated as a finding. In two-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs on a two-cue task, the barrier left after alignment falls with width for every kind of pair. At width 5, pairs that rely on the same cue keep barriers (0 to 0.65 in loss) that overlap those of pairs relying on different cues (0.15 to 0.54), even after an exhaustive search over permutations and rescalings. From width 64, both kinds are connected. Within a width, the barrier falls as the matched units' activations correlate more. Permutations alone leave a barrier between two copies of one function that differ by per-unit rescaling, and quotienting rescaling removes it. A trained curve joins aligned endpoints that the straight line does not, both across the board and in the one flat, poorly connected cell of a load-by-temperature grid, where the accuracy deficit stays. So in this toy, connectedness after alignment is a property of width, of the symmetry group and of the path family, more than of the mechanism.
